newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FEATURE - Venezuelan banks heal, may soon bank again.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Venezuelan banks heal, may soon bank again.

text.p: Only three years after their near collapse brought the economy to its knees, Venezuelan commercial banks are back in the black -- and all without doing much banking.
Survivors of Venezuela's 1994-1995 banking debacle have been able to book handsome profits on passive investments.
Central Bank bills and a canny forex play ahead of Venezuela's devaluation last April have fortified the ragged remains of the banking system.
"But the participation of our banks in the economy is now truly tiny," said a senior source at Venezuela's second largest bank Banco Mercantil, who asked not to be named.
"At the moment, you could fit all of our banks inside Brazil's single largest," he said.
Venezuelan banks have made a quick recovery after swallowing an estimated $11 billion in bail-outs and other support in 1994 and 1995 when half the system collapsed.
The failure in early 1994 of Venezuela's then second largest bank Banco Latino crystallised the crisis which absorbed 15 percent of Venezuela's gross domestic product.

Venezuelans rushed to retrieve savings in a run on deposits as Latino folded. Other banks collapsed as the panic spread. Bankers fled in Lear jets under cover of night. Many are still fugitives abroad, charged with embezzlement and fraud.

Now, by stark contrast, first-half profits are soaring after many banks went long on dollars before an April devaluation that saw the Venezuelan bolivar tumble over 40 percent against the U.S. dollar.
TEMS ARE KEY FACTOR IN REHABILITATION

An even more key factor in the sector's rehabilitation are the Central Bank's high-yielding, low-risk TEM bills -- issued to mop up excess financial liquidity -- that now comfortably pad bank portfolios.
"They don't need to (bank). They've got TEMs," said local InvestAnalysis consultant Alex Dalmady of Venezuela's banks.
Dalmady estimates the Central Bank TEM leg-up has provided the system with an implicit subsidy of $750 million a year.
"Could it have survived without the subsidy? Probably not," he added.

Given the boning-up of bank portfolios, economists agree there is little danger of another systemic financial crisis. And while authorities deny the Central Bank's tacit help in rebuilding the damaged sector "they must be pleased by how it's worked out," said New York-based Bear Stearns analyst Adolfo Sanchez.
Only two years ago, the rubble of the crisis revealed a poorly capitalised, badly managed and loosely supervised system, experts say.
"Most Venezuelan banks didn't really bank back then, at least not as you might understand it," said one vice president at Banco Caribe, generally considered one of Venezuela's best.
"They were more like over-extended holding companies that shuffled funds around phoney shell companies. More than anything, they did it because they could. Everything was hidden."

No more. Banking rules are being revamped and transparency has increased. "Under the new accounting standards, you can actually see consolidated, inflation-adjusted accounts. That's a first," Sanchez said.

Government supervision is tighter, analysts say. Management among surviving banks is more prudent. Provisions for bad loans are higher, rising to 120 percent in August from 95 percent the year before, according to consultants Sintesis Financiera.

And capitalisation rates, the ratio of shareholder equity to net assets and a measure of a bank's leverage, have risen from nine percent at the end of 1995 to 13 percent in August, according to Sintesis Financiera.

That tops the risk-adjusted eight percent required under international standards, although "it's still a bit low when compared to the region...17 percent in Colombia and 20 percent in Brazil," Sanchez said.

Venezuelan banks are mindful and three of the country's biggest and best-regarded -- Banco Mercantil, Banco Provincial and Banco Venezolano de Credito -- have taken advantage of new-found confidence to launch American Depository Receipts (ADRs) to raise fresh capital.
"That would have been impossible before," Sanchez said.
TEMS HAVE DISPLACED LENDING ROLE
TEMs may have saved Venezuela's banks, but they have also displaced banking's traditional lending role for now.
For every bolivar deposited in a Venezuelan bank, only 38 cents are lent, compared to 111 in Colombia, 124 in Mexico and 139 in Chile, Banco Venezolano de Credito figures show.

"That will change as domestic credit demand recovers next year," predicts economist Francisco Vivancos. He sees banks drawing down TEM holdings as demand for loans rises with economic growth. The non-oil sector is projected to grow four percent in 1997, after a steep 3.5 percent drop this year.
Some fear a lending spree given that investments in TEMs and other highly liquid securities topped 40 percent in August, up from 32 percent the year before, and are easily converted into loans.
But most believe Venezuela's crisis is too fresh in the memory of borrowers and lenders. "I don't think there will be lending euphoria," Vivancos said. "The crisis is still too close."

The sector's shrinkage also limits any possible lending binge. Nearly 100 percent inflation since January has whittled away by 32 percent in real terms the sector's current deposit base of some 3.858 trillion bolivars ($8.2 billion), according to financial magazine VenEconomy.

Total loans outstanding now represent some $3.3 billion, less than half the planned annual investment of state-owned oil company Petroleos de Venezuela (PdVSA.) The oil giant's 10-year plan envisions annual investments of some $7 billion.
Banking officials admit they will be unable to take full advantage of that dramatic oil sector growth.
"We can only ever finance a small part, although we have set up an oil industry department, as have many other banks, to finance more marginal activities," the Mercantil source said.
CALLS FOR CONSOLIDATION
With 38 banks, the sector is also begging for consolidation, analysts say, and needs more efficiency.

For example Banco Caracas, a respectable mid-sized bank, has $179 million in deposits spread out over 67 branches. "At $2.7 million per branch, that's not even enough to pay electricity bills," said InvestAnalysis' Dalmady.
Banco Mercantil, for one, has embarked on a cost-cutting programme and is apparently strengthening business outside Caracas where clients tend to be more loyal and harder to reach.
That move comes ahead of the expected reprivatisation of Banco de Venezuela, Banco Consolidado and Banco Latino, three large state-owned banks due to be sold before the end of the year.
Their sale could mark the entry of foreign, highly efficient competitors into the Venezuelan market, with Spain's Banco Santander widely expected to be a successful contender.
That would bring a keen competitive edge for which Venezuelan banks are woefully unprepared.
"The foreigners are going to go straight for the bread-and butter corporate business," said Dalmady. "That'll be good for consumers, but not for banks."
Local bankers complain they are handicapped by regulations that slow any further narrowing of deposit/lending spreads beyond the current 10 percent.
Under present rules, banks must deposit 12 percent of deposits in non-interest bearing Central Bank accounts, plus a further two percent with National State Deposits Guarantee Fund (Fogade).
Rather than penalise banks, Vivancos said: "It might be better to use other instruments to hedge against financial volatility in the Venezuelan economy".

But President Rafael Caldera, mindful of criticism the country may recoup only a quarter of the funds spent propping up banks, has pointed out that he has raised the Fogade requirement to two percent from 0.5 percent.
That would bring in 1.3 trillion bolivars ($2.8 billion) in interest every ten years, he said, adding. "It is the bankers who will pay for the financial aid."
